newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: KEDO to send site survey machinery to N.Korea.
newsitem.headline: KEDO to send site survey machinery to N.Korea.

text.p: A consortium supervising the construction of nuclear reactors in North Korea is scheduled to ship seismology machinery and other instruments to the North despite the crisis over the defection of a Pyongyang official.
A South Korean Foreign Ministry official said the shipment by the Korean Peninsula Energy Development Organisation (KEDO) would leave late on Wednesday.
But he said the defection crisis had delayed plans to send a 30-member site survey team into North Korea.
Hwang Jang-yop, ranked 24th in Pyongyang's hierarchy, has been marooned in Seoul's Beijing embassy since he sought political asylum one week ago.

The KEDO shipment, which includes reactor site survey instruments, would mark the first to the Communist country since a North Korean submarine ran aground on a South Korean beach last September, freezing North-South contacts.
Pyongyang last December apologized for the incident.
This opened the way for KEDO to sign protocols last month with North Korea for building light-water reactors, putting a 1994 agreement between Washington and Pyongyang back on track.
"The shipment is set to leave South Korea later today," said the Foreign Ministry official.
"The survey team will be deployed afterwards. At the moment, safety of the team members is still under consideration."
Last week the ministry said the team, scheduled to stay in the North for five months, would go in on February 22.

KEDO, a consortium led mostly by South Korea, Japan and the United States, is supervising the construction of two light water reactors in the North in exchange for Pyongyang freezing its suspected nuclear weapons programme.
Under the agreement signed in Geneva in October 1994, North Korea promised to dismantle its weapons-grade nuclear programme in return for several light-water reactors.
The official said the machinery was scheduled to be shipped from Pusan, South Korea's southern port, and would arrive at Rajin in North Korea.
